summary: A humorous, tongue-in-cheek parody of grand academic papers about gigabit networks. It claims to propose a new paradigm for the standards track but is a joke. RFC 1217 is a reply in the same spirit.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1216 is an April 1st joke document about the excitement surrounding gigabit networks. It pretends that the answer to rising communication costs is Ultra Low Speed networking, a deliberately slow system for tasks that can wait.

what is the alternating bit protocol
subtitle: An April 1st joke that proposes ultra-low-speed networking as a response to gigabit hype.

tldr.problem: As an April 1st joke, the memo claims that processing and memory costs are falling faster than communication costs, threatening the Internet community with financial ruin.
tldr.mechanism: It proposes Ultra Low Speed (ULS) networking at .01 uGbps, using old protocols such as the alternating bit protocol and favoring good news.
tldr.outcome: This is an April 1st satire of gigabit-network enthusiasm and paradigm-shift arguments, not a real networking proposal.

today: RFC 1216 is an Informational April 1st RFC with no replacement or update listed in the unit metadata. It presents a joke proposal, not a real standard.

sections.title: A Joke Written as a Serious Proposal
sections.content:
RFC 1216 is dated 1 April 1991. It presents itself as a proposal for a new Internet Activities Board standardization paradigm, but the memo's premise and examples make it an April 1st joke document. Its authors are named Poorer Richard and Prof. Kynikos.

The joke targets attention to gigabit networks and the formal language used to announce a new technical paradigm. The memo says it will describe an approach that addresses technical issues within the constraints of economic science.
sections.plainLanguage: This is an April 1st joke presented in the style of a serious standards proposal. It pokes fun at excitement about faster networks and grand claims of a new paradigm.

sections.title: The Memo's Economic Argument
sections.content:
The memo cites a projection that costs per bit and per MIP will fall 99% per decade, while cost per bps will fall 90% per decade. It argues that this difference will compound and bankrupt the Internet community unless a paradigm shift occurs. It also claims that greater processing power creates demand for communication bandwidth but does not pay for it.

This argument sets up the joke's proposed solution: instead of making networks faster, make them extremely slow. The dramatic economic conclusion is part of the memo's satire.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo claims that computer processing will get cheaper faster than communication. Its comic solution is to slow networks down instead of trying to make them faster.

sections.title: Ultra Low Speed Networking
sections.content:
The proposed ULS paradigm focuses on end-to-end datagrams and virtual-circuit services operating in the .01 uGbps region. The memo claims individual circuits could cost less than $.03 per month, and lists uses such as low-priority facsimile with three-hour delivery, glacier tracking, the US postal service, and research contracting. It then names still slower applications, including gravity-wave detectors, the Italian postal service, and the Congressional budget process.

For its technical basis, the memo reasons that gigabit networks need new protocols, so ULS should use old ones. It names the alternating bit protocol, with 1-bit sequence numbers, as a leading contender. A pun on “bad news travel fast” leads to the claim that ULS gives good news priority.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal's network is intentionally very slow and cheap. The memo jokes that it suits delayed messages and that it should deliver good news before bad news.

sections.title: Efficiency as a Problem
sections.content:
The memo says efficiency threatens the chosen ULS operating point. It lists slow-start, fewer errors at lower data rates, and smaller headers, including a 1-bit sequence number in the alternating bit protocol. It calls the resulting improvement “creeping efficiency,” which would move ULS away from its intended slowness.

Its suggested remedies include Forward Error Insertion, negative window scaling factors, new protocol layers, and multiple presentation layers. The conclusion says the road to Ultra Low Speed technology is “long, slow, and easy.” The security section says security issues are not discussed.
sections.plainLanguage: The joke treats better efficiency as a threat because it could make the network too fast. Its proposed fixes are deliberately absurd, and the memo does not discuss security.
